title: MCP — Consume and Expose a Tool

content.goal: Install the MCP tooling for Python.
content.why: MCP is "USB-C for AI tools" — build a tool once as a server, and any MCP-aware agent can use it. (Learned in Phase 9, Ch 13, section 13.1.)
content.verify: The mcp package installs without error. Run `pip list` and confirm it appears.
content.troubleshoot: If the package name differs in your environment, check the current MCP Python SDK docs. The roles — host, client, server — are what matter and do not change.

content.goal: Write a tiny MCP SERVER that exposes one tool. Create mcp_server.py.
content.why: A server EXPOSES capabilities over the standard protocol. This wraps your word-count logic so it is reusable across any MCP host. (Learned in Phase 9, Ch 13, section 13.3.)
content.verify: The server starts and waits, announcing it offers a get_word_count tool. This same server could be consumed by ANY MCP host — your agent, a coding assistant, a chat app.
content.troubleshoot: If FastMCP's import path differs, consult the SDK's current quickstart. The concept — a server publishes tools with described inputs — is stable.

content.goal: Point an MCP-aware host at your server so its tool appears to the agent.
content.why: The reassuring truth: the agent loop is UNCHANGED. A client asks the server what tools it offers and forwards the model's requests. (Learned in Phase 9, Ch 13, section 13.4.)
content.verify: The host lists get_word_count among its available tools, sourced from your server — with no changes to the agent's think-act-observe loop. To the model, the remote tool looks exactly like a local one.

content.goal: Apply MCP security — trust and least privilege.
content.why: MCP does not remove Chapter 6's safety work — it EXPANDS it, because capabilities can now come from parties you did not write. (Learned in Phase 9, Ch 13, section 13.6.)
content.code:
# Security checklist for any MCP server you connect:
#  - TRUST: only connect to servers you wrote or have reviewed (supply-chain risk).
#  - UNTRUSTED TEXT: treat tool descriptions AND results as untrusted — a malicious
#    server can hide instructions in them (indirect prompt injection, Ch 16).
#  - LEAST PRIVILEGE: give each server the narrowest access it needs.
#  - AUTH: never expose a network-reachable server with powerful tools unprotected.
content.verify: You can state, for your own server, why it is safe to trust (you wrote it), and you understand that a third-party server's descriptions and results must be treated as untrusted input.

content.goal: CHECKPOINT — you understand tool interoperability via MCP.
content.why: You have built a reusable tool server and connected it, seeing that the loop is unchanged.
content.verify: All true — an MCP server exposes get_word_count; an MCP host can discover and call it; the agent loop is unchanged by the switch to MCP tools; you can articulate the security stance (trust, untrusted text, least privilege). Next unit adds a specialist SUB-AGENT that the coordinator calls like a tool.
